extracted.intended_audience: academics, journalists, climate scientists, NGO communicators, development practitioners and policy-makers interested in media, climate change and foreign aid
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative dimensions for how media, NGOs, scientists and donors communicate about climate change and how that communication affects public understanding and allocation of foreign aid. Includes guidance for journalistic framing, scientific communication, NGO messaging, aid allocation drivers, and funding mechanisms for adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: place stories in thematic context (vs episodic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should 'place stories in greater "thematic" context, instead of moving from story to story in an "episodic" manner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thematic framing situates individual events within structural, long-term issues (e.g., climate trends, adaptation needs) and can improve public understanding compared with episodic coverage that treats events as isolated. Use thematic context to link stories to broader mitigation/adaptation debates and policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: label quoted sources for potential special interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists can 'work to label those quoted so as to make more clear to readers which statements could be influenced by special interests.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always identify affiliations, funding sources or potential conflicts of interest for quoted experts/advocates so readers can assess motive and credibility; helps distinguish independent science from interest-driven claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: scientists maintain consistent engagement with media and policy actors
rubrics_metrics.description: For scientists, 'more consistent interactions with journalists and policy actors can improve background understanding of each of the groups about others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, two-way engagement builds trust and mutual understanding, improves accuracy of reporting, and helps scientists translate findings into usable policy messages; institutional support and training can facilitate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: use accurate metaphors and analogies in scientific communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists 'can think more deeply about accurate metaphors and analogies that they can use in order to more effectively communicate their findings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metaphors that convey correct scale, uncertainty and causation; avoid misleading or sensational analogies that exaggerate certainty or impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: improve scientific literacy of policy actors and the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy actors as well as public citizens 'can improve their scientific literacy in order to more capably interpret news reports on the science of climate change, as well as stories on climate change mitigation and adaptation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in outreach/education so audiences can better evaluate risk, uncertainty, and policy trade-offs; improves receptivity to nuanced reporting and policy deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_uncritical_catastrophism (be mindful of 'alarmism' critiques)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper cites critiques that NGO/scientific communication has been described as 'catastrophism' or 'alarmism' (Hulme 2006; Ereaut and Segnit 2006), suggesting a need to balance urgency with scientific bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While alarmist language can mobilize action, it invites critique and may erode credibility; communicators should balance compelling messaging with accuracy about uncertainties and avoid exaggerated pejorative qualifiers ('catastrophic', 'irreversible', 'chaotic') unless supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: recognize effectiveness of 'social scares' in mobilizing policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Past research found that 'social scares…accelerate political demands, (and) can be important sources of social change' (Ungar 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that dramatic messaging can prompt political action and funding, but weigh short-term mobilization benefits against possible long-term credibility or engagement costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: newsworthiness driven by drama, immediacy and visuals (selection bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eisensee and Stromberg show massive imbalances: slow-onset disasters (e.g., drought) receive far less coverage than sudden dramatic events; 'for every person killed in a volcano disaster, 40,000 people must die in a drought to reach the same probability of media coverage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and account for media selection biases toward events with immediate, vivid imagery and high casualty counts; communicators should tailor strategies to overcome this bias for slow-onset climate impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: timing and news pressure determine likelihood of coverage and relief
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To have the same chance of receiving relief, the disaster occurring during the highest news pressure must have six times as many casualties as the disaster occurring when news pressure is at its lowest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing relative to competing news events strongly affects media attention and aid; plan advocacy and media outreach to avoid high-news-pressure windows where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: media coverage correlates with increased aid allocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies (Van Belle et al.; Rioux and Van Belle) report that press coverage correlates with aid flows (e.g., one Le Monde article correlated with an additional US$77,000; each New York Times article correlated with US$1.2 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media presence can translate into measurable funding increases, especially grants; use sustained media engagement to raise profile of crises and influence bureaucratic allocation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: bureaucrats and media have reciprocal influence on aid agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: The relationship is reciprocal—'bureaucrats influence the media at the same time as media coverage influences aid flows.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that officials monitor media and can steer coverage, while media can pressure bureaucracies; advocacy strategies should target both journalists and bureaucratic decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: disaster reporting focuses on suffering; relief coverage is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Most disaster coverage focuses on the suffering, and only a small proportion mentioned international relief efforts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure media strategies highlight responses and assistance opportunities (not only suffering), to inform audiences about how to help and to shape donor responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: aid allocation driven by geopolitics, history and donor interests (not only need)
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental aid is driven by geopolitics and colonial/historical ties; predictors included whether recipients voted with donors in the UN and colonial relationships (Kuziemko and Werker 2006; Hicks et al. 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that strategic interests, voting alignment and historical ties influence funding decisions; advocacy must account for political determinants, not only technical need.

rubrics_metrics.name: smaller donors may allocate more on recipient needs than big donors
rubrics_metrics.description: Big donors (U.S., France, UK, EU) often use aid to serve interests, whereas smaller donors (especially Scandinavian countries) base funding more on recipients' needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor fundraising/advocacy approaches to donor type; appeal to moral/technical need with some donors and to strategic interests with others.

rubrics_metrics.name: adaptation_financing should cover incremental/additional climate costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A major problem has been defining what donors should pay for; debate centers on whether donors cover only costs 'additional' over what would have occurred anyway—'Adaptation financing is available only for incremental costs due to climate change.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fund proposals should clearly distinguish baseline development costs from incremental climate-driven adaptation costs to align with donor eligibility criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: portfolio screening and 'climate-proofing' of development projects
rubrics_metrics.description: DFID, World Bank and other agencies have 'screened their project portfolios' for climate sensitivity; reviews found shortages of information and neglect of potential climate damage (Klein et al. 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should implement systematic portfolio screening to identify climate vulnerabilities and 'climate-proof' projects; include internal capacity building and better data collection to support screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: available adaptation funding is currently grossly insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: UNFCCC/Kyoto funds (Least Developed Country Fund, Special Climate Change Fund, GEF trust fund, Adaptation Fund) amount to under $300 million total pledged/provided (as of writing), far below estimated needs (estimates range from $5–41 billion/year depending on method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these funding shortfalls when advocating for new mechanisms and to justify proposals for alternative revenue sources and compulsory funding mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: proposed funding mechanisms require media-supported public education
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals for new funds (global carbon tax, expanded CDM levy, airline levy) 'raise issues of what kind of public education campaign would be needed' and strategic media work (e.g., France's solidarity levy accompanied by press stories and passenger literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design public education and media strategies in tandem with proposed fiscal measures to build legitimacy and public acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: tie donor actions to polluter_pays framing to increase acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Linking taxable actions of wealthy-country consumers (e.g., long-haul flights) to impacts on poor nations is an intuitive application of the 'polluter pays principle' and can increase acceptability of levies/offsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame funding mechanisms in terms of responsibility and compensation; ensure transparent links between levies and concrete adaptation/compensation outcomes to build support.

rubrics_metrics.name: ensure rigorous independent monitoring and long-term control of offsets/levies
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about the legitimacy of voluntary carbon offsets 'suggest the need for rigorous independent monitoring and long-term control.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design oversight, third-party verification and transparent reporting mechanisms for any market-based or levy-derived adaptation funding to maintain legitimacy and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: messaging for fundraising: positive success stories outperform scolding
rubrics_metrics.description: Message testing found that 'positive language telling success stories and "helping individuals and communities help themselves" were seen to be more effective than scolding comparisons of American aid levels or images of suffering children.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hopeful, solution-focused narratives in fundraising and public appeals; emphasize agency, local solutions and measurable impacts rather than guilt or only graphic suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: coalitions_of_NGOs perceived as more trustworthy than government aid channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Polling showed marked skepticism about government-to-government aid, but 'Coalitions of NGOs' were seen as trustable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage NGO coalitions and partnership branding in appeals where public trust in government aid is low; communicate transparency and effectiveness to maintain that trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: donor_fatigue suggests using 'softer-edged' appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: After years of stark imagery, 'donor fatigue' has led agencies to develop softer-edged requests for aid that emphasize hopeful, achievable interventions (e.g., efficient stoves, renewables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft messaging that reduces compassion fatigue by focusing on feasible, positive interventions and local benefits rather than repeated apocalyptic imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: media campaigns can amplify NGO pressure on international financial institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Media has played an important role in amplifying NGO concerns about IFIs (World Bank, IMF), contributing to scrutiny and some reforms (e.g., Polonoroeste and Carajas projects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-targeted media campaigns that expose problematic projects and mobilize public/opinion can affect IFI policies and funding decisions; combine investigative evidence with public storytelling.
